title: The Weapon Only Krishna Could Name
story:
The war was over, and that was when the killing happened.

In the dark hours after the armies had stopped fighting, Ashvatthama, Drona's son, slipped into the sleeping camp of the Pandavas. He moved through the tents meaning to do what would please his master, and he came to the quarters where Draupadi's sons lay asleep. He killed them where they lay. The camp woke to the worst news a camp can wake to, and Draupadi heard of the death of her sons and grieved as a mother grieves.

Krishna went to her and comforted her. "I will wipe away this sorrow of yours, good lady," he said, "with the head of that unworthy son of a brahmin, the assailant who struck without warning." And a promise, once spoken, is a thing that must be carried out.

Arjuna took up the pursuit at once, Krishna himself driving his chariot. The chase ran long across the darkening plain, and the horses were failing, their strength spent, when Arjuna saw the man he hunted stop at last and turn to face him from far off. Ashvatthama was not the kind of man to be cornered without recourse. He was Drona's son, schooled in the secret science of weapons, and he had one weapon left that no arrow could answer. He released it.

The night came apart. A terrible fire blazed up in every direction at once, not a flame to be aimed at or dodged but a burning that filled the sky from horizon to horizon, so that the whole field stood in glare. In that light Arjuna saw himself for what he was: a man without refuge, his horses spent, his weapons useless against a fire that no steel could stop.

He did not reach for another arrow. He turned to the friend beside him, as a man turns in the last extremity, and his cry went up out of the burning: "Krishna, Krishna, mighty-armed one, giver of fearlessness to your devotees — you alone are the rescue of those being burned!" And more than that, in the terror of the moment, he said what his heart had always known: that Krishna was the primal person, the Lord himself, beyond the nature he had made; that the living world was deluded by his power of illusion; that this very descent of his was for the lifting of the earth's burden. "What is this, and from where does it come?" he cried. "O God of gods, I do not know."

Krishna answered calmly, as though the sky were not on fire. "Know this to be the brahma weapon of Drona's son," he said. "He does not know how to recall it. Only an astra can quell an astra."

So Arjuna, touching water as the rite requires, discharged his own weapon to meet it. The two fires met in the middle of the field, wrapped in a storm of arrows, and their meeting was more terrible than either alone. Together they blazed so fiercely that the three worlds stood in peril — the creatures of the earth and the dwellers of heaven alike threatened by that burning, the very order of the worlds about to be consumed.

And then, at Krishna's word, Arjuna withdrew both weapons — his own and the one that had been loosed against him. The two fires sank, the glare drained out of the sky, and the field was night again, quiet in the way a place is quiet after lightning.

Arjuna stood a long while in the dark, trembling from a terror he would not forget. In the camp behind him a mother still wept, and a promise still waited to be kept.
reflection: In the glare of a weapon no arrow could answer, Arjuna's fear turns naturally into worship: he does not ask for a technique but for refuge, and names Krishna the rescue of those being burned. And the rescue comes as Krishna's rescues often do — not by abolishing the crisis but by giving one clear instruction, and then the strength to draw back a fire no one else could recall.
content_note: References Ashvatthama's night killing of Draupadi's sleeping sons and the blazing of divine weapons; the violence is recalled without graphic detail.
next_story_tease: But the camp had not yet delivered its judgment on Ashvatthama.
